paras: The attempted lynching of H. C. Laws was an attack on the night of Saturday, March 11, 1882, in which masked, armed men entered Greenman's Hotel in Linkville, Lake County, Oregon, to seize Laws, a prisoner charged with the murder of a boy named Frank Calavan. They left without the prisoner, but in an exchange of gunfire they killed Deputy Sheriff J. F. Lewis and wounded Justice Wright. The death of an officer defending a prisoner from lynchers was carried by wire across the country, and western papers followed the search for the mob into April.

Laws was accused of shooting the younger of two Calavan brothers in February near Langell valley, close to the line between Lake County, Oregon, and Modoc County, California. The Yreka Journal called him "a noted desperado" and chief of the "Bonanza Regulators," a group it said existed to keep settlers away from Bonanza, and predicted that "the necks of Law and others will not be safe from Judge Lynch." After a posse arrested his son and two other men, Laws was reported to have given himself up and been bound over. By March 11 he was held at the hotel by Lewis and Wright, awaiting an examination set for Monday.

According to the first Jacksonville dispatch to the Portland Oregonian, ten or twelve masked men rode into town at 10 o'clock, entered the hotel hall, and refused an order to halt. In this version Lewis fired first and slightly wounded one of them, and the lynchers returned fire before leaving without Laws.

Fuller particulars came days later from Captain D. J. Ferre, who reached Jacksonville from Linkville. He said seventeen men entered the hotel office and ordered everyone to sit, and the leader took a light and said, "We want the prisoner; come in, boys." The prisoner's guard fired from upstairs, and about then Lewis was shot through the thigh, cutting the femoral artery; he died within five minutes. Wright was hit in the arm as the men in the office jumped through the window, and the lynchers left carrying a wounded man of their own. Ferre's account said it was hard to tell who fired first and blamed the "rashness" of the guard, "a stripling."

Laws's examination went ahead amid fears of another attempt on the 120-mile trip to the county jail at Lake View. The county commissioners offered a $1,000 reward for members of the mob and Lakeview citizens planned to raise another $1,000, but no arrest of any attacker appears in the coverage. Laws himself was later reported "turned loose" for want of evidence, and a Modoc County grand jury declined to indict him, news the Corvallis Gazette headed "A Travetsy on Justice."

The first dispatch ran on March 13 and 14 under headlines such as "Bloodshed in Lake County" in Sacramento, "Lynhers Foiled" in Memphis, and "A Sample of Mob Murder" in Waco, and as a single line in news summaries as far east as Maysville, Kentucky. As it traveled it was garbled: a syndicated column placed it at Jacksonville, Oregon, and the Watertown Republican named the prisoner "H. C. Lewis" and had him firing on the mob from a jail.

In Oregon, the State Rights Democrat reprinted the Oregonian's particulars as "Tried to Lynch Him," calling it "this unlawful and bungling affair." That account also said there was "no sympathy for Laws," called him "the murderer" before his examination, and reserved its regret for the deputy. The Democratic Times wrote that the aim was to "launch him into eternity on short notice," and the Lakeview Examiner called the lynchers "cowardly and cold-blooded." None of the reports gave the race of anyone involved.

The mob numbered ten or twelve in the first wire and seventeen in Ferre's account. The first wire had Lewis firing first, Ferre pointed to the guard upstairs, and the Lakeview Examiner said Lewis was shot while crouching powerless under a mobber's shotgun. Ferre's account supposed the leaders were Modoc County friends of Calavan joined by local cattlemen, the Examiner named Lassen County men, and Big Valley residents claimed they were Laws's friends feigning a lynching, a charge the Yreka Journal said was "not generally believed."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of H. C. Laws
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Armed, masked men rode into Linkville to take a prisoner charged with murder and were called 'lynchers' by every report; they failed to take him but killed the deputy guarding him (A3, A15, A19).

The mob of ten to seventeen men sought to lynch Laws on a murder charge but left without him, so the man they targeted was not killed (A3, A15); the man they killed, Deputy Sheriff Lewis, was shot defending the prisoner, which makes this an attempted lynching with an officer killed, not a completed lynching (A19, A25).

The Jacksonville wire report, the separate particulars from Capt. Ferre, and the later Lakeview Examiner account all agree that a masked mob seeking Laws killed Deputy Sheriff Lewis and wounded Justice Wright without taking the prisoner (A3, A15, A25).

framing.detail: The first dispatch ran nationally under heads such as 'Bloodshed in Lake County', 'Lynhers Foiled' and 'A SAMPLE OF MOB MURDER'.

The Lakeview Examiner said the lynchers acted 'in a cowardly and cold-blooded manner' in killing an officer.
News-summary columns reduced it to one line about an officer killed protecting a prisoner, some misplacing it at Jacksonville or garbling the prisoner's name.

Target: prisoner H. C. Laws (also printed A. C. Laws, C. Laus, H. C. Lawr), not taken. Casualties: Deputy Sheriff J. F. Lewis of Lakeview, killed; Justice Wright, wounded in the arm; an unnamed member of the mob, wounded and carried off.

Masked, armed 'lynchers'; unidentified. Supposed at first to be led by Modoc county, California, friends of the Calavan boy, reinforced by cattlemen from Langell valley and Bonanza; the Lakeview Examiner later said they were Lassen county men from around Bieber and Big Valley; Big Valley people said they were Laws's friends feigning a lynching.

Laws remained in custody and his examination went ahead; he was later reported 'turned loose' for want of sufficient evidence, and the Modoc county grand jury did not indict him for the Calavan killing
